claims.claim: The Articles of Confederation, the first U.S. national framework (in force from 1781), created a weak central government that could not tax or effectively regulate interstate commerce and had no independent executive; amending them required unanimous consent of all thirteen states.
Shays' Rebellion (western Massachusetts, 1786-1787) exposed the confederation's weakness and helped prompt Congress to authorize a convention in Philadelphia in 1787.

Fifty-five delegates met at the Pennsylvania State House in Philadelphia beginning May 1787, chose George Washington to preside, debated in secret, and drafted an entirely new constitution rather than merely revising the Articles; the document was signed September 17, 1787.

The Great (Connecticut) Compromise, credited to Roger Sherman, resolved the representation dispute by creating a bicameral Congress: a House of Representatives apportioned by population and a Senate with two senators per state (equal representation).

The Three-Fifths Compromise counted each enslaved person as three-fifths of a free person for purposes of representation and taxation, increasing the political power of slaveholding states in the House and Electoral College without granting enslaved people any rights.

Article I, Section 9 barred Congress from prohibiting the importation of enslaved people (the Atlantic slave trade) before the year 1808; Congress banned the trade effective in 1808, though slavery itself continued.

The Constitution rests on federalism (power shared between national and state governments), separation of powers into three branches (Congress makes law, the executive enforces it, the courts interpret it), and checks and balances that let each branch limit the others.

These structural ideas drew on Enlightenment thought, especially Montesquieu's argument for separating governmental powers and John Locke's idea that legitimate government rests on the consent of the governed.

Ratification required nine of thirteen states under Article VII; Federalists (who argued their case in The Federalist Papers by Hamilton, Madison, and Jay) supported the Constitution while Anti-Federalists opposed it and objected to the absence of a bill of rights.
New Hampshire became the ninth state to ratify on June 21, 1788, meeting Article VII's threshold; the new government began operating in 1789.
The first ten amendments, the Bill of Rights, were ratified December 15, 1791, guaranteeing freedoms such as speech, religion, the press, and fair legal procedure.

Article V allows amendments proposed by a two-thirds vote of both houses of Congress (or a convention) and ratified by three-fourths of the states; later amendments abolished slavery (Thirteenth, 1865), barred denial of the vote on account of race (Fifteenth, 1870), and extended the vote to women (Nineteenth, 1920).

conflictingEvidence.issue: The exact date New Hampshire became the ninth ratifying state.
positions: New Hampshire's ratification instrument and multiple authorities date its ratification June 21, 1788.
The National Archives 'A More Perfect Union' narrative references July 2, 1788, the date the Confederation Congress formally noted that nine states had ratified.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Used June 21, 1788 as the ratification date (from New Hampshire's own instrument via the Avalon Project); July 2, 1788 is the later Congressional acknowledgment, not the ratification itself. The lesson states the government began operating in 1789.
